level1.text: A detached house has a $6.0\,\text{m}$ long gutter made of coated steel ($\alpha = 12 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$). On a summer day the sun heats the gutter from $15\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ in the morning to $55\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ in the afternoon. By how much does the gutter get longer? Give the answer in millimetres.

An aluminium overhead wire ($\alpha = 23 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$) between two electricity poles is $50.0\,\text{m}$ long at $18\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ on a summer evening. On a frosty night the temperature of the wire drops to $-27\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. Calculate the change in the length of the wire $\Delta l$ with its sign. Give the answer in millimetres.

In a physics lesson a copper tube ($\alpha = 17 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$) is cooled with ice water to $0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, and its length is measured to be $500.0\,\text{mm}$. One end of the tube is fixed in a stand, and a dial gauge is placed against the other end.

Then steam from boiling water is passed through the tube, and the tube warms up to $100\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.

By how much does the tube get longer, that is, by how much does the reading of the dial gauge change? Give the answer in millimetres.

On the roof of a summer cottage sauna there is a black $200.0\,\textsf{l}$ tank from which shower water is drawn. In the morning the temperature of the water is $12\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, and in the afternoon the sun has heated it to $32\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The coefficient of volume expansion of water is $\gamma = 0.21 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$. By how many litres does the volume of the water grow?

The living room window has a $1.5\,\text{m}$ wide pane of ordinary glass ($\alpha = 9.0 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$). On a summer day the sunshine heats the glass from $20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ to $45\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. By how much does the width of the glass grow? Give the answer in millimetres.
The steel lid of a glass jar that is stuck tight often comes loose more easily when hot water is run over the lid for a moment. What is the reason?
level1.answer: The steel lid expands more than the glass when it warms up, so the lid becomes loose around the mouth of the jar.

choices.text: Hot water makes the metal lid shrink, because the particles of the metal move closer to each other when they warm up.
choices.feedback: Wrong: when it warms up, the average distance between the particles grows, so the lid expands and does not shrink.

choices.text: The mouth of the jar gets smaller, because the particles of the glass grow when they warm up and fill the gap.
choices.feedback: Wrong: particles do not grow when they warm up; their average distances grow. In addition, the water is run over the lid, so the glass warms up less than the lid.

choices.text: The steel lid expands more than the glass when it warms up, so the lid becomes loose around the mouth of the jar.
choices.feedback: Correct: the $\alpha = 12 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$ of steel is greater than the $9 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$ of glass, so the warm lid grows more than the glass and becomes loose.

choices.text: Glass and steel expand by the same amount, but hot water makes the edge of the lid slippery.
choices.feedback: Wrong: different materials expand by different amounts, because their coefficients differ. For steel $\alpha$ is greater than for glass.

level1.text: Three samples of the same size, a piece of steel, a glass of water and a balloon full of air (at constant pressure), warm up from $20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ to $30\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. Which sample expands the most in relative terms, and why?
level1.answer: Air, because only weak interactions bind the particles of a gas to each other.

choices.text: Steel, because the particles of a solid vibrate the most strongly when they warm up.
choices.feedback: Wrong: the particles of a solid are bound tightly in place, so the distances between them grow only a little. For steel $\gamma \approx 3\alpha = 36 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$, which is the smallest of the three.

choices.text: Water, because the particles of a liquid can move freely from place to place.
choices.feedback: Wrong: in a liquid the particles are still close to each other and bound to each other, so water expands much less than a gas. The $\gamma = 0.21 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$ of water is much smaller than the value for air.

choices.text: All equally, because the change in temperature is the same for all the samples.
choices.feedback: Wrong: the same change in temperature is not enough; the relative expansion also depends on the temperature coefficient, which is characteristic of the substance. The coefficient is greatest for a gas and smallest for a solid.

choices.text: Air, because only weak interactions bind the particles of a gas to each other.
choices.feedback: Correct: only weak interactions bind the particles of a gas to each other, so the distances between the particles grow easily, and at constant pressure the gas is free to expand. The $\gamma = 3.4 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$ of air is much greater than that of water, $0.21 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$, or that of steel, $36 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$.

level1.text:
A student calculated how much a $2.0\,\text{m}$ long aluminium rod ($\alpha = 23 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$) gets longer when its temperature rises from $15\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ to $65\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The student wrote $\Delta l = 23 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}} \cdot 2.0\,\text{m} \cdot 65 = 3.0\,\text{mm}$ (units left out).

There is an error here. Calculate the change in the length of the rod correctly. Give the answer in millimetres.

level2.text: A flexible bellows section is installed at the end of a straight section of a district heating pipe, and it can take up a change in length of at most $50.0\,\text{mm}$. The steel pipe ($\alpha = 12 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$) is installed at $10\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, and in use its temperature is $90\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. What is the greatest length the straight section of the pipe may have? Give the answer in metres.

A steel kettlebell with a volume of $2.0\,\text{dm}^3$ has been in a garage at $-22\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ on a frosty night. It is brought inside, where it warms to $20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The coefficient of linear expansion of steel is $\alpha = 12 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$. By how many cubic centimetres does the volume of the kettlebell grow? Hint: for a solid $\gamma \approx 3\alpha$.

On an old-style railway, the steel rails ($\alpha = 12 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$) are $25.0\,\text{m}$ long. When the track is built at $12\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, a gap of $7.2\,\text{mm}$ is left between the rails. Assume that the gap closes when a rail has lengthened by the width of the gap. At what temperature does the gap close?

A metal beam used in a bridge structure, with a length of $5.00\,\text{m}$ at $20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, is heated and the change in its length is measured. The graph shows the change in length $\Delta l$ as a function of temperature.

Calculate the coefficient of linear expansion $\alpha$ of the material of the beam in the unit $10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$ and use the table in the lesson to work out which metal the beam is made of (steel 12, aluminium 23, copper 17, all in the unit $10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$). Read the values you need from the graph.

Example data: the table gives the volume of $1.000\,\text{kg}$ of water at different temperatures. The volume calculated from a density table is given to six significant figures, because the changes are small.

a) At which temperature in the table does water take up the least space, and what does that tell you about the density of water at that temperature?

b) Calculate the temperature coefficient of the volume of water $\gamma$ over the temperature range $4\,{}^\circ\text{C} \ldots 10\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ in the unit $10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$. Use the volume at $4\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ as the initial volume.

c) Compare the result with the value $\gamma = 210 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$ valid at $20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ and explain why water differs from other liquids over the temperature range $0\,{}^\circ\text{C} \ldots 4\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ and why the temperature of the water at the bottom of a deep lake in winter is about $4\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.

The answer field takes the result of part b).

Example data: a group used a dial gauge to measure the change in length $\Delta l$ of a $0.800\,\text{m}$ long metal rod when the rod was heated from $20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The reading accuracy of the dial gauge is $0.01\,\text{mm}$.

a) Calculate the temperature coefficient of the length $\alpha$ of the material of the rod in the unit $10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$ using the first and the last point of the table.

b) Work out from the table in the lesson (steel 12, aluminium 23, copper 17, all in the unit $10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$) which metal the rod is made of, and explain why the measurement points do not usually lie exactly on the same straight line.

The answer field takes the result of part a).

data.caption: Change in the length of a metal rod (example data)

level2.text:
A group is planning an experiment in which the temperature coefficient of the length of steel ($\alpha = 12 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$) is measured from a steel tube. At $20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ the tube is $1.00\,\text{m}$ long, and it is heated with steam to $100\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The group intends to measure the length with a tape measure whose reading accuracy is $0.5\,\text{mm}$.

a) Calculate how much the tube gets longer.

b) Explain why the tape measure is not suitable for this measurement, and suggest an instrument with which a small change in length can be measured reliably.

c) How long should the steel tube be so that the reading accuracy of the tape measure is at most $5.0\,\%$ of the change in length, when the change in temperature is the same? Give the answer in metres.

The answer field takes the result of part c).

Example values: steel rods A and B are made of the same steel and are at first at the same temperature. The length of rod A is $4.0\,\text{m}$ and its temperature rises by $10\,\text{K}$. The length of rod B is $2.0\,\text{m}$ and its temperature rises by $30\,\text{K}$. Both rods can expand freely.

How does the change in length $\Delta l$ change when we move from rod A to rod B?

choices.feedback: Correct: $\Delta l = \alpha l_0 \Delta T$, so the change is proportional to both the initial length and the change in temperature. The length is halved (factor $0.5$) and the change in temperature triples (factor $3$), so $\Delta l_\text{B} / \Delta l_\text{A} = 0.5 \cdot 3 = 1.5$.

This takes into account only the change in temperature. The change in length is proportional also to the initial length: rod B has half as many particle spacings, so the same rise in temperature lengthens it less.

This assumes that the same material always expands by the same amount. The material determines only the coefficient $\alpha$. The change in length also depends on the initial length and the change in temperature, and these change in different ways.

This takes into account only the shorter length. The change in temperature of rod B is three times as large, and it increases the change in length in direct proportion, so even the shorter rod lengthens more.

level3.text:
In a farm machine workshop a steel gear is fitted on the axle of a tractor with a shrink fit. The diameter of the central hole of the gear is $75.000\,\text{mm}$ at $20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ and the diameter of the axle is $75.090\,\text{mm}$. For steel $\alpha = 12 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$.

To what temperature must the gear be heated at least so that it fits on the axle? Also justify why the hole gets bigger and not smaller when the gear warms up, and why the gear is held tightly in place after it has cooled.

The thermostat of an old-style electric sauna heater has a bimetallic strip in which copper and steel strips, each $50.0\,\text{mm}$ long, are joined together (copper $\alpha = 17.0 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$, steel $\alpha = 12.0 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$).

As the sauna warms up, the temperature of the strip rises from $20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ to $100\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.

How much more would the copper strip lengthen than the steel strip if they were separate? Give the answer in micrometres, that is, thousandths of a millimetre. Justify which way the joined strip bends.

A $20.0\,\textsf{l}$ steel can for a motorboat is filled to the brim at a filling station with petrol at $10\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ and closed.

On the jetty the sun heats the can and the petrol to $35\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. For petrol $\gamma = 0.95 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$ and for steel $\alpha = 12 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$. The inner volume of the can grows in the same way as the volume of a steel object of the same size.

How many cubic centimetres of petrol would try to overflow if the cap is opened? Justify why a can is not filled to the brim even though the can also expands.

Example data: steel rails ($\alpha = 12 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$) that are $25.0\,\text{m}$ long are to be installed on a track. The table gives the temperature of the rail at the time of installation and the lowest and highest temperatures of the year (the sun heats the rail hotter than the air). Assume, as is usual with railway rails, that the change in the width of the gap is equal to the change in the length of one rail. The gap must not close in summer, and it must not exceed $30\,\text{mm}$ in winter.

a) Calculate the smallest installation gap at which the gap does not close.

b) Calculate the greatest installation gap at which the gap does not exceed $30\,\text{mm}$ in winter.

c) Justify with a calculation why an installation gap of $15\,\text{mm}$ is acceptable when installing at the temperature in the table but not when installing in a winter frost.

The answer field takes the result of part a) in millimetres.

Example data: the glass bulb of a liquid thermometer contains ethanol, whose volume at $10\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ is $1.00\,\text{cm}^3$ and which fills the bulb exactly. The ethanol rises from the bulb into a glass capillary tube with an inner radius of $0.30\,\text{mm}$. Use $\gamma = 1.1 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$ for ethanol and $\alpha = 9.0 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{K}}$ for glass, and assume that the coefficients are constant over the temperature range $10\,{}^\circ\text{C} \ldots 30\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The inner volume of the bulb grows in the same way as an equal piece of glass, and the cross-sectional area of the capillary is assumed to be constant.

a) Calculate how many millimetres the column of ethanol rises in the capillary when the temperature rises from $10\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ to $30\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.

b) By what percentage would the rise be greater if the expansion of the bulb were ignored?

c) Calculate how much water would rise in the same device, and use it to justify why water is not suitable as the liquid of a liquid thermometer.

The answer field takes the result of part a) in millimetres.
